blocks.heading: From coordination to a business effect
blocks.text: A plan gives people a common intended result, but the work still needs to be organised. If two workers repeat the same task while another necessary task is left unfinished, the team may waste effort and miss its deadline. Clear allocation can reduce that duplication when the instructions are understood and the resources are suitable. The reasoning runs from a management action, through what changes in the work, to an effect on the business. It does not mean that having a manager guarantees success: an unrealistic plan or inadequate resources may still prevent completion.

blocks.heading: Using the Friday deadline
blocks.text: In the workshop case, one worker prepares materials while another completes the first stage of the order. By checking progress each afternoon, the manager can notice a delay before Friday. If a worker is available and trained for the delayed task, changing the allocation may help the workshop recover time. Earlier action can therefore improve the chance of meeting the delivery commitment. The effect is conditional: moving an untrained worker to unfamiliar equipment may create mistakes instead. Effective management requires a feasible response to the problem, not simply a decision to move people. A useful explanation names the action, connects it to a case fact, and traces the consequence for the order.

blocks.heading: Keeping the purpose visible
blocks.text: Management is needed to coordinate people and resources around objectives. A reason becomes clearer when the explanation identifies the specific work problem it addresses and the effect that follows.
